HORNET HRU-7

THE FIRE HAS AIR SUPPORT NOW.

HORNET is a heavy-lift autonomous response aircraft built to map, observe, supply, coordinate, and operate inside wildfire environments that routinely deny access to conventional crews and aircraft.

01 / Operational reality

BUILT FOR THE GAP.

Wildfires create a recurring gap between what incident commanders can see, what crews can reach, and what aircraft can safely approach. HORNET is designed to enter that gap.

△

Terrain denied

Roads end. Slopes continue. HORNET does not confuse the limits of a vehicle with the limits of the mission.

◉

Visibility degraded

Smoke, darkness, canopy, and terrain remove certainty. Overlapping sensors put it back on the map.

⌁

Communications fragmented

Ridgelines divide radio networks. HiveLink turns altitude into infrastructure.

00

Time compressed

Built for the minutes before containment becomes evacuation. Some drones take pictures. HORNET takes responsibility.

02 / Selectable architecture

MISSION SYSTEMS.

Six rotors. Twelve eyes. Zero interest in your access road. Select a subsystem to inspect the airframe that nature forgot to patent.

SYSTEM 01 / 08

Compound-Eye Sensor Array

STATUS: OVERQUALIFIED

Multispectral visible, thermal, near-infrared, and low-light imaging with overlapping fields of view.

“This sensor package can find a hot spot through smoke, darkness, tree cover, and three layers of interagency disagreement.”
03 / Mission profiles

ONE AIRFRAME. MANY BAD DAYS.

Designed for environments where helicopters hesitate and humans should not be. When the terrain says no, HORNET says cleared.

01

Fireline Reconnaissance

Maps active edges, spot fires, escape routes, hazards, and changing wind conditions.

02

Communications Relay

Restores connectivity across broken terrain and overloaded incident networks.

03

Precision Resupply

Delivers medical supplies, batteries, tools, hose fittings, food, water, and emergency equipment.

04

Crew Overwatch

Maintains thermal and visual observation around hand crews and equipment.

05

Sensor Deployment

Places temporary weather, air-quality, camera, and fire-behavior sensors.

06

Night Operations

Extends mapping, monitoring, and logistics support into darkness and dense smoke.

07

Coordinated Swarm Operations

Multiple HORNET aircraft divide terrain, share maps, relay communications, and coordinate payload delivery.

ONE HORNET IS A PLATFORM.
TWELVE HORNETS ARE A WEATHER EVENT.

09 / Safety, command, accountability

AUTONOMOUS DOES NOT MEAN UNSUPERVISED.

Every mission remains accountable to human command, aviation rules, payload policy, and the oldest principle in emergency response: somebody has to sign the form.

Human mission approval

Named personnel authorize mission goals, boundaries, and payloads before launch.

Geofencing

Dynamic airspace, incident perimeter, altitude, and exclusion-zone enforcement.

Aviation coordination

Integration with incident air operations and manned-aircraft deconfliction.

Remote override

Positive human intervention and command transfer remain available throughout flight.

Audit logs

Commands, plans, sensor events, model decisions, and overrides are recorded.

Privacy controls

Collection zones, access roles, retention windows, and protected-area rules.

Payload authorization

Physical and software interlocks restrict deployment to approved mission profiles.

Flight termination

Layered lost-link, contingency landing, safe-state, and termination procedures.

Incident data retention

Policy-aligned preservation, review, disclosure, and deletion of operational data.
